question: What is the meaning of battery manufacturer in relation to manufacturer?
description: A battery manufacturer is a specific type of manufacturer, indicating a company or entity that produces batteries as their primary product. In the context of the AgentRole pattern, a battery manufacturer would be an agent playing the role of a producer, focusing on the creation and distribution of batteries. This role is part of the broader manufacturing industry, which encompasses various types of products and manufacturers. The AgentRole pattern allows for the dynamic representation of roles that agents can assume in relation to products, such as being a manufacturer, vendor, certifier, or customer. In this case, the battery manufacturer is an agent specializing in the production of batteries, which is a subset of the manufacturing role.

Article 26
Cases in which obligations of manufacturers apply to importers and distributors
1.
An importer or distributor shall be considered a manufacturer for the purposes of this Regulation and shall be subject 
to the obligations of a manufacturer pursuant to Article 22, where:
(a) it places a product on the market under its own name or trademark;
(b) it modifies a product intentionally or the product is unintentionally modified in such a way that compliance with the 
declaration of performance and conformity, or with the requirements set out in or adopted in accordance with this 
Regulation may be affected;
(c) it makes a product available on the market with a declared use that is different from the declared use attributed by the 
manufacturer in the process of assessment and verification;
(d) it claims for the product characteristics deviating from the characteristics declared by the manufacturer; or
(e) it opts to assume the role of the manufacturer.
2.
Paragraph 1 shall also apply to an economic operator who places on the market:
(a) a used product covered by a harmonised technical specification laying down provisions for used products;
(b) a used product not covered by a harmonised technical specification with provisions for used products and not placed 
on the Union market before;
(c) a remanufactured product.
3.
Paragraph 1 shall not apply where the economic operator only:
(a) adds translations of information supplied by the manufacturer;
(b) replaces the outer packaging of a product already placed on the market, including when changing the packaging size, if 
the repackaging is carried out in such a way that the original condition of the product cannot be affected by it, and that 
any information required by this Regulation is still correctly provided.
4.
An economic operator providing the activities listed in paragraph 3 shall inform thereof the manufacturer or its 
authorised representative, regardless of whether that economic operator owns the products or provides services. It shall 
carry out the repackaging in such a way that neither the original condition of the product nor its compliance with this 
Regulation is affected by the repackaging, and such that any information required by this Regulation is still correctly 
provided. The economic operator shall act with due care in relation to the obligations of this Regulation.
Article 27
Obligations of fulfilment service providers
1.
When contributing to the making available on the market of a product, fulfilment service providers shall act with due 
care in relation to the obligations of this Regulation.
2.
A fulfilment service provider shall make sure that the labelling and documents provided by the manufacturer or 
importer are available or accompany the product, and in particular:
(a) the CE marking and the labelling referred to in Article 22(9);
(b) the declaration of performance and conformity;
(c) the general product information and the instructions for use and safety information referred to in Article 22(6).

A product is usually manufactured by a ‘manufacturer’, sold by 
‘vendors’, certified by ‘certification bodies’, and bought by ‘customers’. 
These roles around the product can change over time and are context- 
specific. The AgentRole pattern is suitable for capturing these dy­
namics, which allows us to separate the ‘Agent’ from the ‘Role’ they are 
playing regarding the product. For example, the manufacturer of a 
product is an agent who plays the role of a producer. This role has a 
temporal extent, which starts at the manufacturing date and continues 
until the discontinuation date of the product model. The ‘certification 
body’ is an agent that performs the role of a certifier for a limited 
‘temporal extent’, which is generally defined by the validity of the cer­
tificate (see Fig. 4). 
The product module also aims to model various aspects of products, 
including their specifications, manufacturing details, and supply chain 
information in order to enable traceability. Products often require 
traceability for supply chain and end of life management, quality 
assurance, and compliance. The ‘Provenance’ pattern is chosen to model 
the history, origin, or source of products, including how they are 
created, modified, and transferred. For example, to trace the product's 
manufacturing process, a ‘ProvenanceActivity’ instance can be created. 
Our ‘Product’ module can be linked to the ‘ProvenanceActivity’ using 
‘generatedBy’. This is addressed by making the Product class a subclass of 
the ‘EntityWithProvenance’. To trace the supply chain, we created a class 
of ‘SupplyChainActivity’ as a subclass of ‘ProvenanceActivity’. A product 
goes through multiple stages: raw material extraction, manufacturing, 
assembly, packaging, shipping etc. Each stage can be modeled as an 
instance of ‘SupplyChainActivity’. Using ‘generatedBy’, the product can be 
linked to these stages, thereby tracking its journey from raw materials to 
consumer. By using the ‘Provenance’ pattern in this manner, it is possible 
to provide a rich historical context to the entities in our DPP ontology, 
which is invaluable for providing information related to traceability, 
accountability, or detailed historical records of products. Fig. 4 shows 
both the product agent and provenance notion. 
Products involve various types of quantities like dimension, weight, 
density, and other similar technical specifications, for which the 
‘Quantity’ pattern is selected. To capture these key attributes, we 
specialized the class of ‘Product’ with the class of ‘ProductSpecification’. 
We introduced a property ‘hasQuantity’ to connect ‘ProductSpecification’ 
with ‘Quantity’. The ‘Quantity’ pattern makes it possible to specify the 
kind or type of the quantity. For example, ‘Length’, ‘Density’ or ‘Weight’ 
would be different kinds of quantities. The numerical value associated 
with a quantity typically consists of a unit and a number. The ‘Quantity’ 
pattern is well suited to capture these attributes in interoperable and 
scalable manner (see Fig. 5). 
A product may have different types or modification of existing types. 
The ‘Explicit Typing’ pattern is selected to explicitly define types for 
each product (see Fig. 5). 
Products often involve instructions such as assembly, disassembly 
and installation. Instructions might not always be simple strings.
